narrative:
The model predicts you have a 19% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your reason for choosing this school, and the fact that you have had no previous class failures. Surprisingly, your clean record with zero past failures actually worked against you in the model’s eyes. Among students who passed, having no failures is the norm, but in your specific combination of circumstances the model interpreted this as meaning you may not have developed the resilience or study habits that come from overcoming earlier setbacks.

Far more influential was your stated lack of interest in higher education. Every single student who passed expressed a desire to continue studying after school, whereas you do not. This absence of long-term academic ambition was the strongest signal pulling the prediction toward failure. Your reason for choosing the school—its reputation—also pushed the outcome in the failing direction. Students who chose the school for its academic reputation were less likely to pass than those who chose it for the specific course offered.

To improve, you should seriously reflect on why you do not want to continue studying and whether that view could change. Even small steps, such as setting clearer short-term goals or seeking guidance on future options, could help shift your trajectory and reduce the need for remedial classes next year.
